boundary_rationale: The row is bounded to the single chazon header verse: “The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.” (web:Isa.1.1). boundary_rationale: The unit opens on the book’s first sung-frame onset, the cohortative “אָשִׁ֤ירָה נָּא֙ לִֽידִידִ֔י שִׁירַ֥ת דּוֹדִ֖י לְכַרְמ֑וֹ כֶּ֛רֶם הָיָ֥ה לִֽידִידִ֖י בְּקֶ֥רֶן בֶּן שָֽׁמֶן” (oshb:Isa.5.1, byte tier), matching WEB’s “Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill.” (web:Isa.5.1) -- a tier-1 addressee/genre shift from the preceding oracle. The love-song frame is then read forensically: the summons “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? The book's very last verse turns from that universal worship to a grim closing image, “They will go out, and look at the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me; for their worm will not die, nor will their fire be quenched” (web:Isa.66.24), rendered "תוֹלַעְתָּ֞ם לֹ֣א תָמ֗וּת" (oshb:Isa.66.24, byte tier) ('their worm will not die'). This couplet is kept as its own unit because it is the book's terminal span (no rear seam follows 66:24) and because its own internal turn -- from universal worship to unending punishment of the transgressors -- is a distinct rhetorical function from the ingathering report that precedes it.
